First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2{z}^{1/2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(1+{x}^{2})}{{z}^{1/2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{1/2}}-2x{z}^{1/2} \\ (1+{x}^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-2xz\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+{x}^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-2xz \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}-\frac{2xz}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,z & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2x/(1+{x}^{2})dx} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2})} \\  & =1+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=1+{x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,z) & =(1+{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}) \\ (1+{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[z(1+{x}^{2})] & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[z(1+{x}^{2})]\,\text{d}x & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ z(1+{x}^{2}) & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

where in the last step we used that $y>0.$
